summary:
California's own care-access law is the most protective element of its record. SB 107, signed by Governor Gavin Newsom in September 2022, made California the first state to declare itself a sanctuary for transgender young people seeking medical care. Young people from other states can obtain hormones and puberty blockers in California, and the law shields families from child-abuse investigations or criminal prosecution for seeking gender-affirming care. The shield covers families who travel to California for that care.

Recorded anti-LGBTQ hostility in California is the highest raw count of any state. The GLAAD ALERT Desk documented more than 1,000 anti-LGBTQ incidents nationwide in 2025, of which California accounted for 198; the next highest state recorded 72. California is the most populous state and no per-capita denominator accompanies the ranking, so the figure is a raw count only and does not establish that a trans visitor faces more risk in California than in a smaller state.

Law-enforcement data show a dramatic increase in anti-LGBTQ hate-crime reports in Los Angeles over the same period.

A July 2026 analysis places California in its "Safest States" law band with a score of 4.1 and 1.9 recorded incidents, and argues that even the most protective law floors do not eliminate recorded hostility.
tangentialFactors:
The two 2025 and 2026 datasets on California measure different things and point in different directions. The GLAAD ALERT Desk figure is a raw total of recorded incidents, in which California leads the country; the July 2026 analysis scores the state's legal protections in its "Safest States" band while recording 1.9 incidents. The analysis's own conclusion is that a protective law floor does not by itself eliminate recorded hostility, which is the reading that accommodates both figures.

California's protective posture on care access and on custody sits against a national framework that has moved in the opposite direction on passports, entry screening and federal facilities. Those national measures belong to the United States record and are not repeated here.
localsOnly:
California's state prison system houses transgender inmates according to gender identity. As of January 2021 it was the only state doing so. Housing is identity-based within the general population, and no transgender-only unit or segregation practice is documented.

California became the first state to fund gender-affirming surgeries for transgender prison inmates in 2015. KPBS reported that year on how the new guidelines would be implemented, covering the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation's operational guidelines for transgender inmates. That coverage confirms an identity-based care and guidance posture and contains no explicit statement of a transgender-only unit or segregation practice.
outOfScopeNotes:
The 2025 incident counts are raw totals. No per-capita denominator appears in the material, so the ranking cannot be read as a per-capita risk comparison between California and less populous states.

The July 2026 analysis gives a score of 4.1 and 1.9 recorded incidents without stating the denominator or the time frame behind the 1.9 figure.

The attribution of the Los Angeles hate-crime increase to the period of the governor's public platforming of anti-trans figures is the publication's framing; no causal finding is documented.

Whether California's identity-based prison housing policy remains in force after January 2021 is not established by the available material; the most recent confirmation is that date. No transgender-only unit or segregation practice in California prisons is documented.

No California-specific material on bathroom and facilities law, entry screening, or gender markers on state documents was identified; those questions are governed by the national framework and by other states' laws.
